name: Hush
subtitle: part two: the first dance
story: Sound is slow on Hush: a shout takes five days to cross the valley, so wedding vows are shouted five days ahead and land on the day. The band forgot. The man who proposed across the valley in March and the woman who walked over with her answer married in the first snow, in the chapel on the far side, and the band played far too loudly. Five days later, at home, they had their first row, about the band. Halfway through, the wedding arrived across the valley, faint and slow: the cheering, the speeches, and then the song from their first dance. They danced. They were still furious.
hook: A planet for couples who bicker.

episode.opener:
They married
in the first snow.

beats.text:
On Hush, songs get home
five days late.

The band was very loud.
Everyone sang along.

Five days later, at home,
their first fight.

It was about the band.
She'd thought it too loud.

Meanwhile, the wedding
was still crossing the valley.

Halfway through,
their first dance arrived.

episode.caption:
The song in the first second is theirs.

This is part two of Hush. In March he shouted a proposal across the valley, and in October she walked over with her answer.

Hush is a long, snowed-in valley where sound crawls along slower than you can walk, and a shout takes five days to cross it. People plan around it. Wedding vows are shouted five days ahead, so they land on the day. The band forgot.

They married in the first snow, in the chapel on the far side, and the band played far too loudly. Five days later, at home, they had their first row. It was about the band. Halfway through, the wedding came drifting in across the valley: the cheering, the speeches, and then the song from their first dance.

I was a guest. I clapped at the end of their first dance, so five days later I also clapped at the end of their row.

(On Earth, sound crosses a kilometre of air in about three seconds, a little longer in the cold. On Hush, allow five days.)

Who said sorry first? Nobody knows yet. It's on its way.

first_comment: The neighbours across the valley get the row next week. They've been told how it ends.

short.kicker: Hush, part two. A planet for couples who bicker.
short.title:
Songs here get home
five days late.

beats.text:
Five days after the wedding,
their first fight.

Halfway through,
their first dance arrived.

name: Tessel
subtitle: part two: the second cake
story: Winter on Tessel lasts a year, with no sun and no calendar, so every village has someone who keeps the date. Jess keeps it on a board by her door, and her wages are the first slice of every birthday cake. The winter she lost count, the village kept the board for her. When she got her chalk back, she checked their sums and found Day 213 on there twice. It was her birthday: the village had wanted more cake. Jess has never let a sum go in her life. She found no mistakes.
cover: Her birthday was on the board twice.

episode.opener:
A year-long winter.
Jess counts it. Exactly.

beats.text:
The board by her door
is the village's calendar.

The winter she lost track,
the village kept it for her.

With her chalk back,
she checked their sums.

Her birthday was on there
twice.

The village wanted
more cake.

Jess has never let
a sum go in her life.

episode.caption:
Count the days on Jess's board.

This is part two of Tessel. In part one, Jess lost count for the first time in her life, and the village kept the board going without her.

Tessel is 90,000 people on a slow, tilted world: winter lasts a year, and summer about a fortnight. With no sun to count by, every village has someone who keeps the date. Jess has kept hers since she was a girl, and her wages are the first slice of every birthday cake in the village.

When she got her chalk back, she checked the village's sums, the way you'd mark homework. Day 213 was on the board twice. It was her birthday. The village had wanted more cake. Jess has never let a sum go in her life. She found no mistakes.

I went to both. I'd only brought one card.

(King Charles has two birthdays: his real one in November, and an official one in June, with a parade. The story goes that George II started it in 1748, because his own birthday was too cold for marching. On Tessel there's no warmer month to move it to, so the village just had it twice.)

Is there a day you'd count twice?

first_comment: Next winter's board already has her birthday down twice. In her own chalk.

short.kicker: Tessel, part two. A planet for the double-checker.
short.title:
A year-long winter.
Jess counts it. Exactly.

beats.text:
Her birthday was on there
twice.

The village wanted
more cake.

name: Ruby
subtitle: part two: the handshake
story: On Ruby, the sky blushes for you: whenever anyone on the planet is embarrassed it goes a little pink, and red when it's bad. Last week the evening newsreader signed off with 'Love you, bye,' and the sky stayed red for a week. On day eight it came back blue, and so did he. He ended the news with a firm handshake, to camera. He didn't blush; he's done twenty years of news. The sky went pink anyway. His teenagers were watching.
cover: His teenagers turned the sky pink.

episode.opener:
Here, the sky
blushes for you.

beats.text:
Last week, the newsreader signed off
with 'Love you, bye.'

On day eight, the sky came back blue.
So did he.

So now, a firm handshake.
To camera.
beats.note: turn: the next beat changes one thing on the identical camera (the sky goes pink)

beats.text:
He didn't blush.
Twenty years of news.
The sky went pink anyway.
beats.note: the house camera from frame 1; the end card follows on it

episode.caption:
Those two outside the house are his.

This is part two of Ruby. Last week the evening newsreader ended the news with 'Love you, bye,' live, to eleven million people. Four million said it back, and the sky stayed red for a week.

Ruby is a small blue planet of twelve million people where the sky does your blushing for you: a little pink whenever anyone is embarrassed, red when it's bad. Everyone can see it, so nobody gets away with anything.

On day eight the sky came back blue, and so did he. He'd had a week to think. At the end of the news he looked down the lens, held out his hand and offered the nation a firm handshake. He didn't blush. He's done twenty years of news. The sky went pink anyway, from a house on the edge of town where his two teenagers had been watching.

I watched it in a café, and shook back. Some of that pink was mine.

(German has one word for being embarrassed on somebody else's behalf: Fremdscham. On Ruby, it's called having a dad.)

When did your dad last turn your sky pink?

first_comment: He's moved on to a salute. His teenagers now watch the news through their fingers.

short.kicker: Ruby, part two. A planet for embarrassing dads.
short.title:
Here, the sky
blushes for you.

beats.text:
The newsreader signed off
'Love you, bye.'

So now, a firm handshake.
To camera.

name: Bramble
subtitle: part two: the first one down
story: Trees on Bramble never stop growing. The tallest has a small rain cloud of its own, and near the top is a village that hasn't come down in six hundred years. It has its own kitchens. Their family on the ground cooks for them anyway, and every evening a pinecone drops with the same answer: 'Coming!' On Wednesday, someone came down. It took him a day. Agnes had the table laid before he touched the ground. He'd already eaten. She poured him a cup anyway.
hook: A planet for the family cook.
cover: The first one down in 600 years.

beats.text: They don't need to.

The village has its own cloud
and its own kitchens.

Their family below
cooks for them anyway.

Agnes has cooked for them
for fifty-one years.

Every evening, a pinecone
comes down with the answer:
'Coming!'

On Wednesday,
someone came down.

It took him a day.
Agnes had the table laid
before he touched the ground.

episode.caption:
Every light up that tree is a kitchen.

This is part two of Bramble. In part one, a village near the top of the tallest tree hadn't come down in six hundred years, and every evening the family on the ground called them for dinner and got the same pinecone back: 'Coming!'

Trees on Bramble never stop growing. It's a day's climb down and a week back up, so nobody bothers, and the village has its own rain cloud and its own kitchens. Agnes has cooked for the top of the tree for fifty-one years anyway.

On Wednesday, someone came down. It took him a day. Agnes had the table laid before he touched the ground. He'd already eaten. She poured him a cup anyway.

I was standing right there. I hadn't eaten. Nobody asked.

(On Earth, a redwood can't pull water much higher than 122 to 130 metres, so that's about as tall as a tree can get; the tallest known, Hyperion in California, is about 116. Bramble's tallest tree is watered from the top.)

Would you have fed him anyway?

first_comment: He had seconds. Then a pinecone landed by his plate: 'Dinner's ready.'

short.kicker: Bramble, part two. A planet for the family cook.
short.title:
Nobody's come down
in 600 years.

beats.text:
Their family
still cooks for them.

Then someone
came down.

name: Summer
subtitle: part two: the dragon
story: On Summer, it snows once every eighty years. By the end, Nan was the only one left who'd seen the last one, and she had mentioned it at every wedding and every funeral for eighty years. Then it snowed again, and it squeaked, as she'd said. Now everyone has seen snow, and everyone mentions it at every wedding and every funeral. Nan has heard enough. At the next wedding, she stood up and said she's seen a dragon.
cover: Nan has moved on to dragons.

episode.opener:
It snows here once
every eighty years.

beats.text:
Only Nan was left
who'd seen it.

She mentioned it at every wedding.
At every funeral.
Then it snowed again.
beats.note: identical camera to the opener; one thing changed: snow. Turn line

beats.text: Now everyone has seen it.

They mention it at every wedding.
At every funeral.

At the next wedding,
Nan stood up.

episode.end: Nan says she's seen a dragon.
episode.caption:
Nan's the one without a parasol.

This is part two of Summer. In part one, it snowed for the first time in eighty years, and Nan, who had been describing the last snowfall since she was six, turned out to be right. It squeaked.

Summer is 210,000 people on a world where it's always summer, apart from one snowfall every eighty years, give or take. Coats are museum pieces, and at school, snow is taught next to dragons.

By the end, Nan was the only one left who'd seen it, and for eighty years she had mentioned it at every wedding and every funeral. Then it snowed again. Now all 210,000 people have seen snow, and they mention it at every wedding and every funeral. Nan has heard enough. At the next wedding, she stood up during the speeches and said she's seen a dragon.

I was at that wedding. I'd just got to the part where it squeaks.

(Earth has dragons. In 1910, rumours of a 'land crocodile' reached a Dutch officer in what is now Indonesia, and he went and got one: the Komodo dragon, up to three metres long. Nobody on Summer has gone to look.)

Do you believe her this time?

first_comment: The school has moved snow to geography. Nobody's touching dragons.

short.kicker: Summer, part two. A planet for competitive nans.
short.title:
It snows here once
every eighty years.

beats.text: Only Nan had seen it.

Then it snowed again.
Now everyone has.

short.end: Nan says she's seen a dragon.

name: Fond
subtitle: part two: the cough
story: On Fond, everyone gets one 'I love you'; say it a second time and it comes out as a cough. Sam spent his on his mum, Kath, at the station, the day he left for the city. In the city he met Maya, and held out until February. Then, on her doorstep, he told her anyway, and it came out as a cough. Maya looked at him for a long time. Then she coughed back. She'd spent hers years ago, on a pony.
cover: His second 'I love you' was a cough.

episode.opener:
Everyone on Fond gets
one 'I love you'.

beats.text:
Say it twice,
and it comes out as a cough.

Sam spent his on his mum,
the day he left for the city.
beats.note: the station, last winter, as in part one: the snow stops as he says it

beats.text:
In the city,
he met Maya.

He held out
until February.
beats.note: identical camera; the snow has gone

beats.text:
Then, on her doorstep,
he told her anyway.
It came out as a cough.
beats.note: identical camera: his cough, warm and jagged, the colour of the real one

beats.text:
Maya looked at him
for a long time.

episode.caption:
His only one goes in the first second.

This is part two of Fond. In part one, Sam left for the city and spent his one 'I love you' on his mum, Kath, on the station platform. She said, 'Take a coat.'

Fond is 880,000 people, long snowy winters and one 'I love you' each. Say it a second time and it comes out as a cough, so people keep theirs and say 'Have you got your keys?' instead.

In the city, Sam met Maya. He held out until February. Then, on her doorstep, he told her anyway, and it came out as a cough. Maya looked at him for a long time. Then she coughed back. She'd spent hers years ago, on a pony called Toffee.

I had a cold the week I was there. Four strangers coughed back.

(The story goes that the novelist Natsume Soseki, teaching English, told a student that nobody in Japan would say 'I love you'; they'd say 'The moon is beautiful, isn't it?' On Fond, you can say that one as often as you like.)

How long would you have held out?

first_comment: Kath has met Maya. She sent them both home with lozenges.

short.kicker: Fond, part two. A planet for mummy's boys.
short.title:
Everyone here gets
one 'I love you'.

beats.text:
Sam spent his
on his mum.

He told Maya anyway.
It came out as a cough.
